Staff is going to do presentations and then we are going to ask questions and then we are going to have stakeholder comments before we go into any of the motions. We used to do carryover motions up

We will then have stakeholder comments on all of the motions and whatever else the stakeholders would like to talk about and then we will go into the committee and go through all of the motions as a single package. and we will do one minute on the clock. It is not a hard and fast rule, just a guide. Please keep your comments as short as possible. I will tell you we had a very good meeting on friday and then another good meeting today on chapter 9. I believe sections 1, two, three and a lot of them modifiability questions related to chapter 7 are covered in motions tonight so there is a consensus among

those we have spoken to friday and today, and county staff, that we don't need the modifiability meeting on wednesday. Unless something radically different happens tonight that MAY require that, and stakeholders please feel free if you think strongly we should have a meeting on wednesday, please feel free to say so in the comments and we will discuss that but for now the plan is to cancel the meeting on wednesday unless

something changes. So with that and without further ado, if I could ask staff to do the presentation on chapter 7, that would be great. thank you and good evening, board. I am rick hancock and will be presenting this item for chapter 7, development standards. Development standards is part of, in chapter 7 this is part of the continuing zoning ordinance reorganization so this chapter would include many regulations for the first time in their

own chapter as opposed to separate zoning regulations. So we are including site development, lot requirements, open space has its own section now. Treeplanting, replacement, preservation requirements, parking requirements is also in this chapter. Transportation requirements for vehicles,

bicycle and pedestrian routes. And additionally, utilities and specific sewer and water but all types of utilities. The owners associations like homeowners and property owners associations had their own section and are treated similarly throughout the zoning ordinance now. It also includes the development option for the legacy a three and a
10 zoning districts. As we

mentioned briefly part of the reason we put these development standards in this chapter is to provide them consistently throughout the county with particular emphasis, I would say, for open space, utilities, and owners associations. Currently depending on the district, there are some nuances and a little bit different way we take a look at these things. We want to take a look at them from a countywide basis. We have also updated many of the standards such as clarifying the relationship between buffer yards and setbacks. Sometimes those terms get confused and we have also

up dated some of the lot frontage and access requirements to be more modern. For the first time we have also included transition standards so that when new development goes in, they are a better neighbor to the developments that are previously existing. In the issues identified in the report, there are a few so I would like to go through these briefly. Open space is a new section to treat open space and

we have standardized how open space is calculated. Part of this is based on the general plan concepts of open space so what we are really trying to do is get quality open space. We do this particularly in table 7-02-02 by assigning factors based on the characteristics of the open

space. You have 100% or a bonus factor for environmentally sensitive areas and public dedications, for example, for parks. There is the 100% factor for most of your open space types. And then finally there is a 50% to reduce marginal open space or

off-site open space. We do allow, particularly with the approval of a special exception, to be able to provide some of your open space off-site that needs to be limited to half and would only count for 50%. There have been some things that we've worked through. It has received a fair amount of public comment during the public review and the planning commission and even since the planning commission. So we have worked

with many of those who have made comments and we have a solution. One of those is to allow a project wide approval for open space. So if you get a concept development plan approved you can identify where the open spaces can be provided instead of being stuck at each end every individual site plan which MAY or MAY not fit with the entire

development. We are also used to exempt facilities from the requirement. Proposed modification of the required open-space amount for redevelopment, where the previous approvals or previous requirements were for a lower amount of open space, so this would be up to the board's discretion where they can say no, you need to provide the

full amount, or the board can say you know what? Let's just get the same amount of open space that was previously required for redevelopment only. We have also added some flexibility to the types of open space. So for example, buffers and screens. We are less concerned with width than we are with the type and how it screens so we would like to

shift that. We've also added a new type of open space called supplemental landscaping. If you cannot meet the minimum 20 foot dimension you don't get 0 value. You get a 50% value, so it's less, and it has to still be an average of 10' wide and at least 400 ft.|. And then we

also proposed to remove the restriction on certain types of open space to no more than 50% of required open-space with the notable exception of being the off-site open space which would still be limited to that 50% requirement. Then we also have some language to clarify that only required open-space is subject to an easement and there are only some very specific requirements that

trigger that requirement. We can get into that if you would like over discussion. There's another issue we would like to bring to your attention and receive direction. That is the planning commission decided to increase the setbacks along route seven from the fairfax county line to the broad run to 75' for

parking and 100' for building. This previously was reduced down to 50' in 2007 and there have actually been a few projects that have been approved since that time, one of them shown here on the screen which, as you can see, would not exist in the present configuration at all if this were to be adopted. The reason why staff is bringing this to

your attention is that there is not any general plan guidance. There's nothing in the general plan relating to setbacks and we see this as a deviation from board established policy and we wanted to highlight that. We also have some changes to the use buffer matrix in section 7.04.03. When this was drafted it was converting existing requirements. But as you know there have been a number of changes to the use

requirements in chapters 3 and four so how we are categorizing uses does not really lineup with how we had treated them with me put this regional matrix together. Another issue is that it is really implemented by a zoning administrator opinion in 2019 when these sections were most recently up dated. What we are

proposing to do is revise some of the names and characteristics of these groups . It reduces the number from 13 to 12 but we are also thinking of adding an appendix, appendix d based on classification of grouping of land uses as provided in chapter 3. This way, everybody from staff to the applicant can know, depending on the use that they are proposing, what those
buffer requirements are going

to be. We also have three additional uses with regards to parking. I do not have motions in the packet regarding these. We are anticipating some additional discussion perhaps on wednesday which MAY not happen, so for these three items we will be coming forward at a tentative later meeting with motions representing these items. One is residential parking ratios. Generally the planning commission increased a lot of the residential parking

requirements. They did break the uses out a little differently. They currently exist in revised 93. They look at dwellings, single-family attached or multi family stacked. Number of bedrooms whether it is one, two, or three and also the size of the garage. If it is a one or two car garage and felt like there were different parking demands

based on that. Additionally the size of the lot. Sore for a single-family detached on a narrow lot there is not as much street frontage so there would be less available on the streets of the planning commission felt like there should be additional requirements to make sure that there is still enough provided for the entire neighborhood. We would like to note that there are lower parking ratios in the urban zoning district so even though generally there are more in urban, there are less and staff has a clarifying issue with what is existing in

the zoning ordinance to have some ambiguity on a single-family attached when it has a one-or 2-car garage as it only relates to the two dwellings. Parking for attainable housing, the draft ordinance provides for automatic reductions based on the affordability limits. I

have had a productive discussion with kim hart and we have an alternative parking reduction for multi family attached ahu units which can function a little bit differently than your generic attainable housing so we will be coming forward to you with a proposed staff motion to adopt

a flat rate option for ahu multi family attached. Additionally, even though these are automatic reductions, other reductions are still available. Based on location, and presenting a parking adjustment as any other project would be able to. Finally for electronic vehicle parking, the planning commission draft includes ev parking only if a

project meets three requirements. One is that a parking adjustment is approved, two is that it is in an urban, suburban, or industrial district and is at least 10,000 ft.| of building addition. However, it does not give amounts. It just says parking is required. So what we will be looking forward to is

direction to add amounts, percentages. We are looking at 10% for residential and lodging uses, 2% for commercial, civic, and industrial uses and no ev requirements for other types of uses. Included in your packet is the revisions that we have to the utility section. We've had quite a bit of revisions since the planning commission

adopted the draft zoning ordinance and, well we considered a lot of things. To address concerns from loudon water and other county departments and some of the changes made to chapters 3 and four. This at dates the water and sewer standards in zoning districts, it better implements the leesburg ama zoning

districts which is revise with the 2019 general plan and also requires central water and sewer for new development in the transition zoning districts. And of course, staff does have a few quality control revisions that we think make the zoning ordinance better. This concludes my presentation and I am happy to do my best to answer your questions. thank you MISTER Hancock.

Please put your lights on. Supervisor briskman? thank you. On slide five, I am a little bit confused. Are you indicating that if a project has environmentally sensitive areas and or public dedication areas, that they get 150% credit?
essentially yes. It is a carrot approach to getting the types of open space that we are looking forward to. So for example if there are wetlands on site, or an historic

element, like we know that this is an important place we want to preserve, we give them a bonus credit for that. so that means they get 100% credit +50%? essentially if there is an acre of that it would count as an acre and a half I need to read the definition again but I mean, wetlands aren't necessarily usable. aren't necessarily developable but they can be developed over and currently under the revised, the current zoning ordinance you get the same credit if you pave over
the wetlands and landscape it with non-wetlands as you do if you kept the wetlands so we are trying to encourage keeping the environmental benefits.

okay, all right. And then on slide 9, and I to read this correctly that we are increasing the requirements for parking on sfa/sfd multifamily attached -- that is a generalization. There are a variety of more, different categories of residential uses and also we

provide different rates based on the type of zoning district that it is in. If it is in urban versus rural. I'm running out of time. least it was brought up during the public hearing. we will probably be in touch on that because I think a garage could count -- should count as a full space because if we have space we have to increase asphalt on the rest of the project and I don't know that is enforceable. to both residential and commercial districts? yes, that would apply to any of the parking ratios that exist. If a project is, they can apply for a special exception or a z mod to reduce those rates. We have an administrative procedure so that if they provide transportation studies and showing that they do not need parking, then it can be approved by the zoning

administrator. Now, it is capped at 35% so anything more than that would have to go to a special exception. I assumed the parking issue was going to stay with us for a little bit.

Is there anything, any changes to the industrial areas on parking standards? Those of us that have those know there are truly constant issues going on with vehicles. And what happens is, while you are looking, when you have a building, say, a flex building with five different auto uses, they each get five or six spots. It's nowhere near adequate. They've got

customers coming and going, cars that can't move, so it spills out all over the place, out into the street. You talk to the sheriff's office and they do a ton of, they write a lot of tickets and that kind of stuff so were there any changes to those? we did actually add a standard particularly for the auto repair. So to draw a distinction between storage of vehicles and parking

requirements, you cannot store the vehicle. You can't have a vehicle that you are doing work on in a required parking space. It has to be above and beyond. I believe we do the same thing for sales so if you are selling automobiles there is a parking requirement but that is exclusive of your display area. okay and then the last 15

seconds I will go to the can of worms that is affordable. the open space requirements for public dedication, what is public dedication, what does that entail? Is that anything donated for public use or does it have to be recreational? there is actually more than one so obviously public dedication is a lot of things.

On ev requirements suburban. Would that be in public parking? Is that chargers? Is that what you are referring to? That was not clear to me.

in a commercial center for example if they got a parking reduction and they were over 10,000 ft.| they would have to provide ev parking which is infrastructure so you can park there. I've got it, thank you. two areas, again, parking. Of course it is always parking.

I don't want to, in any way make it more difficult for affordable housing developers to build affordable housing. But based on my observations in leesburg, not necessarily elsewhere, we can often have a one-bedroom apartment with an entire family living in it,

potentially, with two working folks both of whom have cars. A two-bedroom will sometimes have two entire families, four cars, a three-bedroom, three entire families, potentially six cars. So we don't always match what I think our assumptions here might be as

far as parking needs. We had a small rambler in leesburg and one story, probably a two-bedroom rambler and every evening we would have about nine vehicles parked on that lot. So our constituents are not necessarily living the way this might assume they are. So

I wonder, when we looked at the parking needs, did anybody go around and say what are the parking needs in this subdivision or this townhouse community for apartment lock? We also have a lot of spillover from apartment units onto the neighborhood streets has resulted in the town having to put in place residential parking restrictions but there

just seems never to be enough parking. I wonder where are we as a can see no additional parking space that is not utilized? I don't see it in leesburg and it could just be my district that does not experience this the way that I think we assume it would in this rewrite. Any thoughts on that? I think that was

particularly why the planning commission spent so much time on parking. They received a number of concerns and it's always when the project comes up, there's not enough parking. Generally for your residential projects. So that's why generally there is an increase in the parking that is required and they also looked at only counting garage spaces as half of space. They felt maybe 50% on a good day are using garages for parking so

it's just exacerbating the problem. With regards to affordable housing that was also part of the reason why they felt that the reductions based on affordability was probably a safer bet. However, we have received projects that have been approved and provided parking studies and surveys of ahu multi family attached which showed that it was about

1 1/2 spaces or less per unit. That included projects, I believe, in leesburg but all the most recently approved multi family affordable projects in the county were included in that study. So there is some science behind that number but some of these -- anyway. We've thought about it a lot, yes.

okay, thank you. thank you, chair turner. is unsafe for them to drive because of all of the large vehicles that are parked on the side of the road. I think that is one of the issues that I am seeing and if we have tried to help alleviate the problem that my constituents are calling me about. difficult to get hard, fast scientific numbers on this, because a lot of this depends on how far you are willing to walk. Are you willing to put up with a parking ticket every so often? And how do you determine the best way to put these numbers so that everyone is happy and you don't use up too much land area for parking. It is certainly a balancing act. As far as homeowners associations, we don't have anything that

there MAY be something that we want to do with this because I don't want to see the parking in front. I want to see it on the side or in the back. conversely right now the draft ordinance sets us back 100' for a building and 75 for parking from fairfax to route 28. one to speak we are going to talk about parking, I spoke at your first public hearing asking for the garage space to be counted as a full parking space. appreciate help with that. People not using the garage and parking illegally. We do also support the motion for the alternative option for parking for ahu's 's. recognize that households -- but it adds asphalt to projects. That not only increases overall cost and disincentivize is the use of garages in dwelling units which is integral for design in urban and suburban districts but leads to real stormwater implications. specifically as well. good evening members of the board. I build attainable housing and I'm addressing issue number five on housing which is the ratio for attainable housing. is an unfortunate reality. I wish it were different but I hope you will consider these thoughts. our final speaker is MISTER Myers. hi, I am representing while the conservation stakeholders.
